title: The path of return
hook: teshuvah: recognize, regret, confess, resolve; read in full next year

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chamber of secrets, and your line: neither knows. Did you give something with your name left off? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-one.

"O Israel, return unto the LORD thy God." The prophet Hosea calls it out, and the word he uses, return, runs through Jewish prayer. Tradition reads Hosea's call on the Shabbat between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and names that Shabbat for it. And return is the subject Maimonides chose to close his Book of Knowledge. A week and more ago, we noticed that the opening book of his code ends with a way back. Today we walk up to that path and look at how he describes the steps.
screen: `RETURN UNTO THE LORD THY GOD.` → `A WORD ALL THROUGH JEWISH LIFE.` → `THE BOOK OF KNOWLEDGE ENDS HERE.`

segments.voice: The path of return. In Hebrew, teshuvah. Not quite repentance; more like turning around, coming back. Maimonides asks plainly: what is teshuvah? And he answers with steps. Turn it four ways. First, recognize and leave. The person stops doing the wrong thing, and takes it out of their thoughts. You can't turn from a road you won't admit you're on. Second, regret. The person is sorry for what was done. Not a passing wince, but real regret, looking back. Third, confess. Maimonides says the person must put it into words, out loud, saying what was done. Earlier, at the very start of these laws, he describes those words: I did this, I am sorry, I am ashamed, I will not do it again. Spoken, not only felt. Fourth, resolve. The person commits never to return to that act. And Maimonides adds a striking test: the One who knows all hidden things can bear witness that this person won't go back. The resolve has to be real all the way down. Then one more line, which matters a great deal. For wrongs done to another person, Maimonides says, turning to God is not enough. A person must repair what was harmed, and seek the other person's forgiveness. The path of return runs through the people we hurt. Next year, this path reads these laws in full. Today, just the outline of the road: recognize, regret, confess, resolve.
screen: `RECOGNIZE AND LEAVE IT.` · `REGRET WHAT WAS DONE.` · `SAY IT ALOUD.` · `RESOLVE NOT TO RETURN.` · then, large: `THE PATH OF RETURN.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to name one thing to turn from. Settle, and breathe. Let one habit or one act come to mind, something small and true. A sharp tone. A shortcut. A silence where you owed a word. Don't pile on. Just one. Recognize it. Notice whatever regret is there, without drowning in it. If it's safe and private, say it once, quietly, in plain words. Then picture the next time it might come up, and see yourself turning the other way. The bell holds the time.
The path of return. Teshuvah: in Maimonides' laws, recognizing and leaving a wrong, regretting it, saying it aloud, and resolving not to go back. Today's word.
Your line: the path of return. Today, if there's someone you've wronged, even slightly, take one step toward repair: a message, an apology, a thing put right. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Jews practice teshuvah all year, and especially in the month of Elul and the Days of Awe before Yom Kippur, when it is customary to seek forgiveness from people one has wronged before asking it of God.

notes: Hosea 14:1 quoted from the KJV (14:2 in Hebrew and JPS numbering); used because the JPS 1917 wording was not certain. Consider replacing with JPS 1917 if a Keeper can confirm it.

The index's four steps (recognize, regret, confess, resolve) are mapped onto 2:2; Maimonides' own order is abandon, remove from thought, resolve, regret, then confess. Please confirm the mapping is fair.
Shabbat Shuvah is named for the haftarah from Hosea 14; 'gives its name to the Shabbat between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur' is stated. Please confirm.
'Next year, this path reads them in full' follows the index hook; please confirm the year-five outline.
